# Gauge theories {#sec-gauge-theories-chapter}

A gauge theory makes a global symmetry local: the derivative is replaced by a covariant derivative containing a gauge field, whose curvature is the field strength. Electromagnetism is the abelian case and Yang-Mills theory the non-abelian one. A symmetry of the equations need not be a symmetry of the ground state, and when a gauge symmetry is broken spontaneously the gauge fields acquire masses: the Higgs mechanism. The chapter has three parts, gauge invariance, symmetry breaking and lattice gauge theory.

The first part starts from the phase rotation of a complex scalar, shows why making its angle position-dependent forces a new vector field on us, and builds electromagnetism from that requirement: the gauge field, the covariant derivative, the field strength and Maxwell's action. It then replaces the phase rotations by the matrices of a non-abelian Lie group, and the same construction gives Yang-Mills theory, whose field strength contains a commutator and whose gauge fields interact with each other. The second part asks what happens when the lowest-energy state of a theory is less symmetric than its equations: the vacua form an orbit of the symmetry group, every broken generator gives a massless Goldstone boson, and when the broken symmetry is a gauge symmetry the Goldstone bosons are absorbed and the gauge bosons become massive. The third part puts the gauge field on a Euclidean lattice as parallel transporters along the links, shows that Wilson's action tends to the Yang-Mills action, solves the $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $U(1)$ and $SU(2)$ theories in two dimensions and at strong coupling, where large Wilson loops obey the area law of confinement, and proves Elitzur's theorem that a local symmetry cannot break spontaneously.

The chapter comes after quantum field theory and builds on it. Electromagnetism has already appeared in vector form in
@sec-electromagnetism and in covariant form in @sec-complex-vector-fields; quantum field theory has quantised the free
fields, shown that a massive vector is consistent only if it acquires its mass through a Higgs mechanism
(@def-higgs-consistency), quoted the running of the gauge coupling that makes Yang-Mills theory asymptotically free
(@exm-rn-asymptotic-freedom), and outlined the chiral anomaly (@def-chiral-anomaly). This chapter supplies the classical
gauge theories behind those statements: the gauge field and its covariant derivative, the Yang-Mills action, and the
symmetry breaking that gives the gauge bosons their masses. The renormalisation chapter that follows uses both: the Ward
identities of quantum electrodynamics rest on gauge invariance, and asymptotic freedom on the Yang-Mills theory built
here.

Every statement is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty with folded solutions; each part ends with three integrative exercises. The conventions are those of the rest of the book: the signature is $(+, -, -, -)$, so that Maxwell's Lagrangian is $-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(\vec E^2 - \vec B^2)$ and a vector mass term is $+\tfrac12m^2A_\mu A^\mu$; a field of charge $q$ has the covariant derivative $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + iqA_\mu$; Lie algebra generators are anti-Hermitian, $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ for $SU(2)$, with $\operatorname{Tr}(T_aT_b) = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$; and the masses of scalar fluctuations are read from the second derivatives of the potential.

## Gauge theories {#sec-gauge-theories}

A gauge theory makes a global symmetry local by introducing a connection, the gauge field, whose curvature is the field strength; electromagnetism is the abelian case and Yang-Mills theory the non-abelian one. This part has two sections. Abelian gauge invariance starts from the phase symmetry of a complex scalar, defines local symmetries, the gauge field, the covariant derivative and the field strength, and ends with Maxwell's action. Yang-Mills theory repeats the construction for a non-abelian group, where the field strength acquires a commutator, the equations become nonlinear and a constant potential can carry a field strength; the Bianchi identity is the structural identity that every such field satisfies.

### Abelian gauge invariance {#sec-abelian-gauge}

A global phase rotation of a charged field is a symmetry; making its angle depend on position breaks the
symmetry, and restoring it requires a new field, the gauge potential, whose own dynamics is electromagnetism.
This section defines local symmetries, the covariant derivative, the abelian gauge field and its field strength,
following @alvarezgaume2005 [Sec. 4.3] in our conventions, and it is the pattern that Kaluza-Klein theory derives
from geometry in Part III. It starts from the gauge transformation of the potentials (@def-emm-gauge-transformation) and the
minimal coupling of a charged particle (@def-emm-minimal-coupling) of the electromagnetism chapter, and shows that they
are the abelian case of a general construction.

#### Global and local symmetries

A continuous symmetry of a Lagrangian was defined in @def-continuous-symmetry-fields as a transformation of the fields depending on a parameter. The distinction that founds gauge theory is whether that parameter is a single number for the whole of spacetime or a function that may take a different value at each point. The definition names the two cases.

::: {#def-global-local-symmetry}
#### Local symmetry

A symmetry (@def-continuous-symmetry-fields) with a constant parameter is called **global**; it is
**local** (a **gauge symmetry**) if the parameter is instead an arbitrary smooth function $\alpha(x)$. A global symmetry
relates different field configurations; a local symmetry relates different descriptions of the same physical
configuration, as a change of coset representative does in @sec-coset-vielbeins.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The simplest global symmetry is the phase rotation of a complex scalar, which we met as the source of a conserved particle number. It is the running example of the whole section, and the first example recalls why it is a symmetry.

::: {#exm-global-phase}
#### The global $U(1)$ of the complex scalar

$\phi \mapsto e^{i\alpha}\phi$ with constant $\alpha$ leaves $\partial_\mu\bar\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi - m^2|\phi|^2$
invariant (@exm-symmetry-phase); its Noether charge is the particle number of @exm-current-u1.
:::

Letting the angle depend on the point is the natural next step, and it fails for a reason worth understanding. The derivative of the rotated field contains the derivative of the angle, and that extra term spoils the invariance of the kinetic term.

::: {#exm-local-phase-fails}
#### The local phase rotation fails

With $\alpha(x)$, $\partial_\mu(e^{i\alpha}\phi) = e^{i\alpha}(\partial_\mu\phi + i\partial_\mu\alpha\,\phi)$, and the
kinetic term picks up terms proportional to $\partial_\mu\alpha$ (@exr-complex-phase-rotation, @fig-gauge-covariant):
derivatives compare the field at neighbouring points, whose phases have been rotated by different angles.
:::

Local symmetries are not an exotic feature of electromagnetism: every field theory written on a manifold has one. The third example identifies coordinate invariance as a local symmetry and the Levi-Civita connection as its gauge field.

::: {#exm-local-coordinate}
#### Coordinate changes as local symmetries

General coordinate transformations of a field theory on a manifold (@sec-tensor-fields) are local symmetries
with the diffeomorphism as parameter, and the Levi-Civita connection is the gauge field that makes derivatives
covariant (@sec-covariant-derivative): gauge symmetry and coordinate invariance are the same structure.
:::

![Why a local phase rotation needs a gauge field. Top: the phase arrows of $\phi = e^{i\theta(x)}$ (blue) and of
$e^{i\alpha(x)}\phi$ (red), rotated by a different angle at each point; the ordinary derivative compares arrows in
different frames. Bottom: the position-dependent angle $\alpha(x)$ and the shift $-\alpha'(x)$ of the gauge
field that compensates the extra term in $\partial(e^{i\alpha}\phi)$. Generated by
`figures/gauge_covariant.sage`.](figures/gauge_covariant.svg){#fig-gauge-covariant width=75%}

{{< interactive gauge_covariant 460 >}}

The interactive version above applies the rotation $\alpha(x) = a\sin x$ to a field with a background gauge field and lets the amplitude $a$ vary. The ordinary derivative of the rotated field changes with $a$, while the covariant derivative introduced below keeps its modulus; the first exercise computes the change of the free Lagrangian exactly.

::: {#exr-gth-local-phase-kinetic}
#### The change of the free Lagrangian

Compute, with Sage in $1 + 1$ dimensions, the change of $\mathcal{L} = \partial_\mu\bar\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi -
m^2|\phi|^2$ under $\phi \mapsto e^{i\alpha(x)}\phi$, and express it through the Noether current $j^\mu =
i(\bar\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi - \phi\,\partial^\mu\bar\phi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding $(\partial_\mu\bar\phi - i\partial_\mu\alpha\,\bar\phi)(\partial^\mu\phi + i\partial^\mu\alpha\,\phi)$ gives
$$
\delta\mathcal{L} = -\partial_\mu\alpha\,j^\mu + \partial_\mu\alpha\,\partial^\mu\alpha\,|\phi|^2 ,
$$
a term linear in $\partial\alpha$ coupled to the current and a quadratic one; the mass term is untouched. Both
vanish for constant $\alpha$, as they must. These two terms are exactly what the coupling $-qA_\mu j^\mu$ and the
seagull term $q^2A_\mu A^\mu|\phi|^2$ of @exm-covariant-scalar-ed cancel.

{{< sage exr-gth-local-phase-kinetic >}}
:::

The same failure looks different in real components, and seeing it there makes clear that nothing depends on the use of complex numbers. The second exercise rewrites the global phase rotation as a rotation of two real fields.

::: {#exr-gth-global-real-pair}
#### The phase rotation in real components

Write $\phi = (u + iv)/\sqrt2$ with real $u, v$. Show that $\phi \mapsto e^{i\alpha}\phi$ is the rotation of $(u, v)$ by
the angle $\alpha$, that the free Lagrangian is $\tfrac12(\partial u)^2 + \tfrac12(\partial v)^2 - \tfrac12m^2(u^2 + v^2)$,
and find the terms that a position-dependent angle adds to it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{i\alpha}(u + iv) = (u\cos\alpha - v\sin\alpha) + i(u\sin\alpha + v\cos\alpha)$, the rotation matrix acting on
$(u, v)$; and $|\partial\phi|^2 = \tfrac12[(\partial u)^2 + (\partial v)^2]$, $|\phi|^2 = \tfrac12(u^2 + v^2)$, which are
rotation invariant for constant $\alpha$. With $\alpha(x)$, the derivative of the rotated pair is the rotated
derivative plus $\partial_\mu\alpha$ times the rotated $(-v, u)$, so the kinetic term gains $\partial_\mu\alpha\,(u\,\partial^\mu
v - v\,\partial^\mu u) + \tfrac12\partial_\mu\alpha\,\partial^\mu\alpha\,(u^2 + v^2)$: the same two terms as in
@exr-gth-local-phase-kinetic, since $j^\mu = v\,\partial^\mu u - u\,\partial^\mu v$ in these components.
:::

Quantum mechanics already contains a local phase symmetry once the electromagnetic potentials are included. The third exercise works it out for the Schrödinger field, where the coupling to $\Phi$ and $\vec A$ is the familiar minimal substitution.

::: {#exr-gth-schrodinger-gauge}
#### The Schrödinger field

For $\mathcal{L} = i\bar\psi\,\partial_t\psi - \tfrac{1}{2M}\nabla\bar\psi\cdot\nabla\psi$, show that $\psi \mapsto
e^{iq\alpha(t, \vec x)}\psi$ is not a symmetry, and that replacing $\partial_t \to \partial_t + iq\Phi$ and $\nabla \to
\nabla - iq\vec A$ with $\Phi \mapsto \Phi - \partial_t\alpha$, $\vec A \mapsto \vec A + \nabla\alpha$ restores it. Relate
this to $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + iqA_\mu$ with $A_\mu = (\Phi, -\vec A)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Under the rotation, $\partial_t\psi \mapsto e^{iq\alpha}(\partial_t\psi + iq\partial_t\alpha\,\psi)$ and $\nabla\psi \mapsto
e^{iq\alpha}(\nabla\psi + iq\nabla\alpha\,\psi)$, so $\mathcal{L}$ gains $-q\partial_t\alpha|\psi|^2$ and gradient terms.
With the substitution, $(\partial_t + iq\Phi)\psi$ becomes $e^{iq\alpha}(\partial_t\psi + iq\partial_t\alpha\,\psi + iq\Phi\psi -
iq\partial_t\alpha\,\psi) = e^{iq\alpha}(\partial_t + iq\Phi)\psi$, and likewise $(\nabla - iq\vec A)\psi$ transforms
by the phase alone; every term of the Lagrangian is then invariant. The Lagrangian contains $-q\Phi|\psi|^2$, the
potential energy of a charge $q$, and $\tfrac{1}{2M}|(-i\nabla - q\vec A)\psi|^2$, the kinetic energy with the
momentum $\vec p - q\vec A$. Since $A_0 = \Phi$ and $A_i = -A^i$, $D_0 = \partial_t + iq\Phi$ and $D_i = \partial_i -
iqA^i$: these are the components of @eq-covariant-derivative-u1, and the transformation of $(\Phi, \vec A)$ is $A_\mu
\mapsto A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha$.
:::

#### The gauge field and the covariant derivative

The extra term $i\partial_\mu\alpha\,\phi$ can be cancelled only by something that shifts by $\partial_\mu\alpha$ when the phase is rotated. That something is a vector field with its own transformation law, defined next; its shift is the gauge transformation.

::: {#def-gauge-field-u1}
#### Abelian gauge field

An **abelian gauge field** is a vector field $A_\mu$ (@def-vector-field-spacetime) with the **gauge
transformation** $A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha$ whenever the charged fields are rotated by $e^{i\alpha(x)}$
(the sign is a convention; @alvarezgaume2005 [eq. 4.70] writes $A_\mu \to A_\mu + \tfrac1e\partial_\mu\alpha$ with
the opposite sign of the charge). It is the gauge potential of a connection on a principal $U(1)$-bundle
(@def-gauge-potential), and @eq-gauge-transformation for $G = U(1)$ is this transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The electromagnetic potential is the gauge field of the phase symmetry, and its familiar gauge freedom is the transformation just defined. The first example translates between the four-vector and the potentials $(\Phi, \vec A)$ of vector calculus.

::: {#exm-gauge-field-em}
#### The electromagnetic potential

$A_\mu = (\Phi, -\vec A)$ of @exm-vector-electromagnetic is the gauge field of electromagnetism; the familiar
freedom $\vec A \mapsto \vec A + \nabla\lambda$, $\Phi \mapsto \Phi - \partial_t\lambda$ is $A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu -
\partial_\mu\lambda$, the gauge transformation with $\alpha = \lambda$ (up to the charge).
:::

Gauge fields also arise from geometry, where the gauge transformation is a change of coordinates. The second example anticipates the off-diagonal metric components of a five-dimensional metric.

::: {#exm-gauge-field-kk}
#### The Kaluza-Klein gauge field

In Part III the off-diagonal metric components $g_{\mu 5} = A_\mu$ transform under the coordinate change $y \mapsto y +
\alpha(x)$ of the fifth coordinate exactly as @def-gauge-field-u1 prescribes: the $U(1)$ gauge symmetry is a
remnant of five-dimensional coordinate invariance.
:::

A gauge field can also live on a curved space and be defined only chart by chart. The third example finds one on the sphere, in the change of representative of the coset $SU(2)/U(1)$.

::: {#exm-gauge-field-r-connection}
#### The $R$-connection of a coset

On $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$ the one-form $e^3 = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ shifts by $d\psi$ under a change of representative
(@exm-r-connection-gauge): it is an abelian gauge field on the sphere, the monopole potential of @sec-hopf.
:::

The gauge freedom of the potentials is used constantly to simplify computations, and the physical fields must not notice it. The first exercise checks that the electric and magnetic fields are gauge invariant.

::: {#exr-gth-em-gauge-fields}
#### Gauge invariance of $\vec E$ and $\vec B$

Show that $\vec E = -\nabla\Phi - \partial_t\vec A$ and $\vec B = \nabla \times \vec A$ are unchanged by $\vec A \mapsto
\vec A + \nabla\lambda$, $\Phi \mapsto \Phi - \partial_t\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\vec B \mapsto \vec B + \nabla \times \nabla\lambda = \vec B$, since the curl of a gradient vanishes. $\vec E \mapsto -
\nabla\Phi + \nabla\partial_t\lambda - \partial_t\vec A - \partial_t\nabla\lambda = \vec E$, since the time and space
derivatives of $\lambda$ commute. Both statements are the gauge invariance of $F_{\mu\nu}$ of @prp-covariant-u1,
whose components are $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ (@exr-gth-maxwell-from-fields).
:::

A gauge is chosen by imposing a condition on the potential and solving for the gauge parameter that achieves it. The second exercise brings a concrete potential to the Coulomb gauge.

::: {#exr-gth-coulomb-gauge}
#### Reaching the Coulomb gauge

For $\vec A = (tx^2, xy, 0)$ and $\Phi = 0$, find $\lambda$ with $\nabla\cdot(\vec A + \nabla\lambda) = 0$, give the new
potentials, and check with Sage that $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ are unchanged.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla\cdot\vec A = 2tx + x$, so $\lambda$ must solve $\nabla^2\lambda = -(2t + 1)x$; the choice $\lambda = -tx^3/3 -
x^3/6$ works. The new potentials are $\vec A' = (-x^2/2, xy, 0)$, divergence-free, and $\Phi' = -\partial_t\lambda =
x^3/3$: the Coulomb gauge has moved the time dependence from $\vec A$ into $\Phi$. The fields are $\vec E = (-x^2, 0,
0)$ and $\vec B = (0, 0, y)$ in both gauges.

{{< sage exr-gth-coulomb-gauge >}}
:::

A potential with vanishing field strength is not always a gauge transform of zero: the topology of the space can prevent it. The third exercise finds the obstruction on a circle, where it is measured by the holonomy.

::: {#exr-gth-pure-gauge-abelian}
#### Flat potentials and holonomy

Show that $A = d f$ has $F = dA = 0$. On the circle with angle $\theta$, show that $A = c\,d\theta$ has $F = 0$ but is
not $df$ for a function $f$ on the circle unless $c = 0$, and that the phase $e^{iq\oint A} = e^{2\pi iqc}$ acquired
by a charge $q$ transported once around is gauge invariant. When can $A = c\,d\theta$ be removed by a gauge
transformation with $e^{iq\alpha}$ single-valued?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d(df) = 0$. On the circle every two-form vanishes, so $F = 0$ for every $A$; but $c\,d\theta = df$ would require $f
= c\theta + \text{const}$, which is not a function on the circle unless $c = 0$, since $\oint df = 0$ while $\oint
c\,d\theta = 2\pi c$. Under $A \mapsto A - d\alpha$ with $\alpha$ a function on the circle, $\oint A$ is unchanged,
so the holonomy $e^{iq\oint A}$ is gauge invariant. If only $e^{iq\alpha}$ needs to be single-valued, $\alpha =
c\theta$ is allowed when $qc \in \mathbb{Z}$, and then it removes $A$; this is the case where the holonomy is $1$.
Otherwise the flat potential is physical: it is the Aharonov-Bohm phase.
:::

With the gauge field in hand the derivative can be repaired. The covariant derivative adds to $\partial_\mu$ a multiple of the gauge field chosen so that the two shifts cancel, and the definition records the result.

::: {#def-covariant-derivative-u1}
#### Covariant derivative

The **covariant derivative** of a field of charge $q$ is
$$
D_\mu\phi = \partial_\mu\phi + iqA_\mu\phi ,
$$ {#eq-covariant-derivative-u1}
which transforms as the field does, $D_\mu(e^{iq\alpha}\phi) = e^{iq\alpha}D_\mu\phi$, when $A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu -
\partial_\mu\alpha$: the extra term $iq\partial_\mu\alpha\,\phi$ from the derivative is cancelled by the shift of
$A_\mu$ (@prp-covariant-u1, @fig-gauge-covariant). It is the covariant derivative of @def-covariant-derivative-vector
for the $U(1)$ connection, with $\Gamma$ replaced by $iqA$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The first use of the covariant derivative is to make the complex scalar gauge invariant. Replacing $\partial_\mu$ by $D_\mu$ in its Lagrangian gives scalar electrodynamics, whose new terms are the couplings to the gauge field.

::: {#exm-covariant-scalar-ed}
#### Scalar electrodynamics

Replacing $\partial_\mu$ by $D_\mu$ in the complex scalar Lagrangian gives $\overline{D_\mu\phi}\,D^\mu\phi - m^2|\phi|^2$,
gauge invariant (@exr-covariant-derivative-u1); expanding, the terms linear in $A_\mu$ are $-qA_\mu j^\mu$ with $j^\mu$
the Noether current of @exm-current-u1, and the quadratic term $q^2A_\mu A^\mu|\phi|^2$ is the **seagull** coupling.
:::

The same replacement applied to the Dirac field gives quantum electrodynamics. The coupling is again the current times the potential, here without a quadratic term since the Lagrangian is first order in derivatives.

::: {#exm-covariant-dirac}
#### Quantum electrodynamics

$\bar\psi(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m)\psi$ with $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + ieA_\mu$ is the Dirac Lagrangian coupled to
electromagnetism; the coupling $-e\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi A_\mu$ is the electron current times the potential, the
vertex of quantum electrodynamics.
:::

Different fields can carry different charges, and the charge is the integer or real number that tells how the field responds to the phase rotation. The third example collects the rules for products and neutral fields.

::: {#exm-covariant-charges}
#### Fields of different charges

A field of charge $q$ transforms with $e^{iq\alpha}$ and couples through $iqA_\mu$; the product of fields of charges
$q_1, q_2$ has charge $q_1 + q_2$, and a neutral field has $D_\mu = \partial_\mu$. In Part III the charge is the
momentum $n/R$ around the fifth dimension, automatically an integer multiple of a unit.
:::

The covariant derivative of a field has a counterpart for a point particle, where the gauge field enters the momentum.
The fourth example takes the classical charged particle of @maggiore2023electrodynamics [Sec. 8.6.2] and shows which
of its momenta is gauge invariant.

::: {#exm-gth-canonical-momentum}
#### Canonical and kinetic momentum

A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ in the potential $A_\mu = (\Phi, -\vec A)$ has the action $S = \int(-m\sqrt{1 - v^2} -
q\Phi + q\vec v\cdot\vec A)\,dt = -m\int ds - q\int A_\mu dx^\mu$. Its canonical momentum is $\vec P = \partial L/\partial\vec v = \vec p + q\vec A$
with $\vec p = m\vec v/\sqrt{1 - v^2}$ [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, eq. 8.78]. Under $A_\mu \to A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha$ the action
changes by $q\int d\alpha$, a boundary term, so the equations of motion are gauge invariant, while $\vec A \mapsto \vec A + \nabla\alpha$ shifts $\vec P$ by $q\nabla\alpha$
and only the kinetic momentum $\vec p = \vec P - q\vec A$ is physical. In a field theory $-i\nabla$ plays the role of $\vec P$, and
$-iD_i = -i\nabla - q\vec A$ is the kinetic momentum, as in @exr-gth-schrodinger-gauge and @exr-gth-int-plane-wave.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The covariance of the covariant derivative is a short computation that is worth doing once with full care. The first exercise does it with Sage, together with the gauge invariance of the scalar Lagrangian and the identification of the current.

::: {#exr-covariant-derivative-u1}
#### Scalar electrodynamics with Sage

Check that $D_\mu\phi$ transforms covariantly, that $\overline{D\phi}\cdot D\phi$ is gauge invariant, and read off
the current coupled to $A_\mu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-covariant-derivative-u1 >}}
:::

The covariant derivative obeys a Leibniz rule in which the charges add, and this is what makes the charges of composite fields well defined. The second exercise proves it.

::: {#exr-gth-product-charges}
#### Charges of products

Let $\phi_1, \phi_2$ have charges $q_1, q_2$. Show that $\bar\phi_1$ has charge $-q_1$, with $D_\mu\bar\phi_1 =
\overline{D_\mu\phi_1}$, that $D_\mu(\phi_1\phi_2) = (D_\mu\phi_1)\phi_2 + \phi_1D_\mu\phi_2$ when the product is given
charge $q_1 + q_2$, and conclude that $\bar\phi\,\phi$ is neutral and $\partial_\mu(\bar\phi\,\phi) = \overline{D_\mu\phi}\,\phi +
\bar\phi\,D_\mu\phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\bar\phi_1 \mapsto e^{-iq_1\alpha}\bar\phi_1$, so its charge is $-q_1$ and $D_\mu\bar\phi_1 = \partial_\mu\bar\phi_1 -
iq_1A_\mu\bar\phi_1 = \overline{D_\mu\phi_1}$ for real $A_\mu$. The product transforms with $e^{i(q_1 + q_2)\alpha}$, and
$\partial_\mu(\phi_1\phi_2) + i(q_1 + q_2)A_\mu\phi_1\phi_2 = (\partial_\mu\phi_1 + iq_1A_\mu\phi_1)\phi_2 +
\phi_1(\partial_\mu\phi_2 + iq_2A_\mu\phi_2)$. For $\phi_1 = \bar\phi$, $\phi_2 = \phi$ the total charge is $0$, so $D_\mu =
\partial_\mu$ on the product and the Leibniz rule gives the last identity: gauge-invariant composites are
differentiated with ordinary derivatives.
:::

The Dirac Lagrangian becomes gauge invariant in the same way, and the computation also fixes the sign of the coupling and shows that the density coupled to $A_0$ is positive. The third exercise does it in two dimensions with explicit gamma matrices.

::: {#exr-gth-dirac-gauge}
#### Gauge invariance of the Dirac Lagrangian

In $1 + 1$ dimensions with $\gamma^0 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^1 = i\sigma_2$, check the Clifford relations, show with Sage
that $\bar\psi(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m)\psi$ with $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + iqA_\mu$ is invariant under $\psi \mapsto e^{iq\alpha}\psi$,
$A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha$, and read off the coupling to $A_\mu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\gamma^0)^2 = 1$, $(\gamma^1)^2 = -1$ and $\gamma^0\gamma^1 + \gamma^1\gamma^0 = 0$, so $\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} =
2\eta^{\mu\nu}$. The phase cancels between $\bar\psi = \psi^\dagger\gamma^0$ and $\psi$, and $D_\mu$ is covariant, so the
Lagrangian is invariant. The terms linear in $A$ are $-q\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi A_\mu$; the density $\bar\psi\gamma^0\psi =
\psi^\dagger\psi$ is positive, so a positive $q$ means a positive charge density sourcing $\vec E$ in Gauss's law.

{{< sage exr-gth-dirac-gauge >}}
:::

#### The field strength and Maxwell's action

A gauge field is a new dynamical field and needs its own kinetic term. Its building block must be gauge invariant, and the antisymmetrised derivative of $A_\mu$ is the natural candidate, since the shift $\partial_\mu\alpha$ drops out of it; the definition introduces it together with Maxwell's action.

::: {#def-field-strength-u1}
#### Maxwell action

The **field strength** $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$ (@def-field-strength-abelian) is gauge
invariant, because the second derivatives of $\alpha$ commute (@prp-covariant-u1), and it is the commutator of
covariant derivatives, $[D_\mu, D_\nu]\phi = iqF_{\mu\nu}\phi$. The **Maxwell action**
$$
S = -\frac14\int d^4x\,F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = \frac12\int d^4x\,(\vec E^2 - \vec B^2)
$$ {#eq-maxwell-action}
[@alvarezgaume2005, eq. 4.62] is the unique gauge-invariant quadratic action for $A_\mu$ with at most two
derivatives, and its Euler-Lagrange equations are $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = 0$ (@exm-el-maxwell).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Coupling the Maxwell action to charged matter turns the field equations into Maxwell's equations with sources. The first example reads them off and shows that gauge invariance makes the conservation of the current automatic.

::: {#exm-maxwell-equations}
#### Maxwell's equations

$\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = j^\nu$ with the current of the charged matter are Gauss's and the Ampère-Maxwell laws, and
$dF = 0$ the remaining two (@exm-vector-field-strength); the conservation $\partial_\nu j^\nu = 0$ follows from the
antisymmetry of $F$ and is the Noether conservation of @sec-noether-currents, which gauge invariance makes
automatic.
:::

A mass term for the gauge field would be the simplest addition to the Maxwell action, and gauge invariance forbids it. The second example records this, which is the problem the Higgs mechanism of the second part solves.

::: {#exm-maxwell-mass}
#### No mass term

$m^2A_\mu A^\mu$ is not gauge invariant, so a gauge field is massless: the photon has no mass, and giving a mass
to a gauge boson requires the Higgs mechanism of @sec-higgs. The mass term is what the Kaluza-Klein modes of the
gauge field acquire in Part III, through exactly that mechanism.
:::

On a sphere the field strength can be well defined while the potential is not, and the mismatch between charts quantises the charges. The third example is the magnetic monopole on $S^2$.

::: {#exm-maxwell-monopole}
#### The monopole on the sphere

The Hopf potential $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ has $F = -\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ (@def-hopf-connection), a
radial magnetic field of total flux $-4\pi$; the gauge field is defined only chart by chart, with the transition
function $e^{2i\varphi}$ (@exm-transition-hopf), and the charge $q$ of any field must make $e^{2iq\varphi}$
single-valued: Dirac's quantisation condition.
:::

The statement that the field strength is the curvature of the covariant derivative is the computational heart of the definition. The first exercise derives it by expanding the commutator.

::: {#exr-commutator-covariant}
#### The commutator of covariant derivatives

Show that $[D_\mu, D_\nu]\phi = iqF_{\mu\nu}\phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_\mu D_\nu\phi = \partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi + iq\partial_\mu(A_\nu\phi) + iqA_\mu\partial_\nu\phi - q^2A_\mu A_\nu\phi$;
antisymmetrising in $\mu\nu$, the second derivatives of $\phi$ and the $A_\mu A_\nu$ term cancel, the terms
$iqA_\nu\partial_\mu\phi + iqA_\mu\partial_\nu\phi$ are symmetric and cancel, and what remains is $iq(\partial_\mu A_\nu -
\partial_\nu A_\mu)\phi = iqF_{\mu\nu}\phi$: the field strength is the curvature of the $U(1)$ connection
(@def-curvature-connection).
:::

The sign of the Maxwell Lagrangian depends on the signature, and in $(+, -, -, -)$ it is the minus sign that makes the electric energy positive. The second exercise checks the identity with $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ for a general potential.

::: {#exr-gth-maxwell-from-fields}
#### Maxwell's Lagrangian in terms of $\vec E$ and $\vec B$

With $A^\mu = (\Phi, \vec A)$, $A_\mu = (\Phi, -\vec A)$, $\vec E = -\nabla\Phi - \partial_t\vec A$ and $\vec B = \nabla\times\vec
A$, show with Sage that $F^{i0} = E^i$, $F_{12} = -B^3$ (and cyclically), and $-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} =
\tfrac12(\vec E^2 - \vec B^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{0i} = \partial_tA_i - \partial_iA_0 = -\partial_tA^i - \partial_i\Phi = E^i$, and raising one time and one space index
gives $F^{i0} = -F^{0i} = F_{0i} = E^i$. $F_{12} = \partial_1A_2 - \partial_2A_1 = -(\partial_1A^2 - \partial_2A^1) = -B^3$.
In $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ the six mixed components contribute $2\sum_i F_{0i}F^{0i} = -2\vec E^2$ and the spatial ones
$2\sum_{i<j}F_{ij}^2 = 2\vec B^2$, so $-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(\vec E^2 - \vec B^2)$.

{{< sage exr-gth-maxwell-from-fields >}}
:::

The quantisation of charge in the presence of a monopole is the most striking consequence of a gauge field that exists only chart by chart. The third exercise derives Dirac's condition.

::: {#exr-dirac-quantisation}
#### Dirac quantisation

On the sphere with the monopole potential $A = g\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ of charge $g$, show that a field of charge
$q$ is well defined on the overlap of the two charts only if $2qg \in \mathbb{Z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The regular potentials on the two charts are $A_\pm = g(\cos\theta \mp 1)\,d\varphi$, differing by $2g\,d\varphi =
d(2g\varphi)$, so the transition function is $e^{2iqg\varphi}$ (@exm-hopf-connection-monopole); it must return to
itself after $\varphi \to \varphi + 2\pi$, which requires $2qg \in \mathbb{Z}$. The Chern number of @def-chern-number
is $2g$ in these units, an integer, and the charges are quantised in units of $1/2g$.
:::

Maxwell's equations have a source, and the source enters the action through a coupling to the potential, which is
not gauge invariant term by term. The fourth exercise shows that gauge invariance of the coupling and conservation
of the current are the same condition [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, Sec. 8.6.2].

::: {#exr-gth-source-gauge}
#### Gauge invariance requires a conserved current

For an external current $j^\mu$, show that $S = \int d^4x\,(-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} - A_\mu j^\mu)$ is invariant under $A_\mu \to A_\mu -
\partial_\mu\alpha$ for all gauge functions $\alpha$ of compact support if and only if $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$. Derive its field equations
and show that they force $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$ independently.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{\mu\nu}$ is invariant (@prp-covariant-u1) and the coupling changes by $\int\partial_\mu\alpha\,j^\mu = -\int\alpha\,\partial_\mu j^\mu$ after
integration by parts, the boundary term vanishing for compactly supported $\alpha$ [@maggiore2023electrodynamics, eq. 8.75].
This vanishes for all $\alpha$ exactly when $\partial_\mu j^\mu = 0$. The Euler-Lagrange equations are $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = j^\nu$
(@exm-maxwell-equations), and $\partial_\nu\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = 0$ by antisymmetry: a non-conserved source is inconsistent with
Maxwell's equations, for the same reason that it spoils gauge invariance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The gauge invariance of the field strength is the one structural fact on which the whole abelian theory rests. It is an identity in the derivatives of the potential and of the gauge parameter, and it holds because mixed second derivatives commute; the proposition states it in that form.

::: {#prp-covariant-u1}
#### Gauge invariance of the abelian field strength

$F_{\mu\nu}$ is unchanged by $A_\nu \to A_\nu + \partial_\nu\alpha$ when $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\alpha =
\partial_\nu\partial_\mu\alpha$, as an identity in the derivatives of $A$ and $\alpha$; the covariant derivative
$D_\mu\phi$ transforms like $\phi$ (@exr-covariant-derivative-u1).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** An identity in the jet variables.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.FieldTheory.abelian_F_invariant >}}

**Sage.** The covariance of $D_\mu\phi$ is checked by exact computation in Sage (`figures/gauge_covariant.sage`).
:::

A concrete potential and gauge parameter show the cancellation term by term. The first example uses a two-dimensional field with a non-polynomial gauge parameter, so that each derivative produces several terms.

::: {#exm-gth-F-invariance-explicit}
#### An explicit cancellation

In the $(t, x)$ plane take $A_t = 0$, $A_x = tx$, so $F_{tx} = \partial_tA_x - \partial_xA_t = x$. With $\alpha = \sin(tx)$,
$A'_t = x\cos(tx)$ and $A'_x = tx + t\cos(tx)$, and
$$
F'_{tx} = x + \cos(tx) - tx\sin(tx) - \bigl(\cos(tx) - tx\sin(tx)\bigr) = x :
$$
the two derivatives of $\alpha$ produce the same terms, $\partial_t\partial_x\alpha = \partial_x\partial_t\alpha$, and they
cancel (@exr-gth-F-invariance-sage).
:::

Different gauges for the same field strength are not a curiosity but a practical tool. The second example gives two standard potentials for a constant magnetic field and the gauge transformation between them.

::: {#exm-gth-F-landau-symmetric}
#### Two gauges for a uniform magnetic field

The potentials $\vec A_{\rm sym} = \tfrac{B}{2}(-y, x, 0)$ (symmetric gauge) and $\vec A_{\rm L} = B(0, x, 0)$ (Landau
gauge) both have $\nabla\times\vec A = (0, 0, B)$. They differ by $\vec A_{\rm L} - \vec A_{\rm sym} = \tfrac{B}{2}(y, x, 0)
= \nabla(\tfrac{B}{2}xy)$, a gradient, so they are related by a gauge transformation, and the uniform field
$F_{12} = -B$ is the same in both (@exr-gth-landau-symmetric). The symmetric gauge is adapted to rotations about the
$z$-axis, the Landau gauge to translations along $y$.
:::

The proposition can be read as a statement about finitely many numbers at one point, and in that form the role of the symmetric second derivatives becomes explicit. The third example rewrites it in this way.

::: {#exm-gth-F-lean-reading}
#### The identity at one point

At a point, treat the first derivatives $\partial_\mu A_\nu$ and the second derivatives $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\alpha$
as independent real numbers (the jet variables), with the hypothesis that the matrix of second derivatives of
$\alpha$ is symmetric. The conclusion is that the antisymmetrisation of $\partial_\mu(A_\nu + \partial_\nu\alpha)$ equals that of
$\partial_\mu A_\nu$. Without the hypothesis the statement is false, and the failure is physical: a multivalued
$\alpha$ such as an angle has non-commuting derivatives at its branch point (@exr-gth-F-needs-symmetry).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** This is the form of the Lean statement `KaluzaKlein.FieldTheory.abelian_F_invariant`: the jet variables are real variables and the symmetry of the second derivatives is a hypothesis.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.FieldTheory.abelian_F_invariant >}}

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The two gauges of the uniform magnetic field are related by an explicit gradient. The first exercise finds it and checks that the field strength is unchanged.

::: {#exr-gth-landau-symmetric}
#### From the symmetric to the Landau gauge

Find $\lambda$ with $\vec A_{\rm sym} + \nabla\lambda = \vec A_{\rm L}$ for the potentials of @exm-gth-F-landau-symmetric and
check that the magnetic field is unchanged. Is there a gauge in which $\vec A = B(-y, 0, 0)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla\lambda = \tfrac{B}{2}(y, x, 0)$ gives $\lambda = \tfrac{B}{2}xy$. The curl of $\nabla\lambda$ vanishes, so $\vec B$ is
unchanged. $B(-y, 0, 0)$ has curl $(0, 0, \partial_x0 - \partial_y(-By)) = (0, 0, B)$ as well, and it is reached from
$\vec A_{\rm sym}$ with $\lambda = -\tfrac{B}{2}xy$: the second Landau gauge, adapted to translations along $x$.
:::

The invariance can also be computed symbolically for a completely general potential in four dimensions, together with the explicit cancellation of the first example. The second exercise does both, with Sage doing the algebra.

::: {#exr-gth-F-invariance-sage}
#### The proposition with Sage

For general functions $A_\mu(t, x, y, z)$ and $\alpha(t, x, y, z)$ check that all components of $F_{\mu\nu}$ are unchanged
by $A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu + \partial_\mu\alpha$, and redo @exm-gth-F-invariance-explicit.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Sage's symbolic derivatives of a general function commute, so the check is the identity of the proposition with
the symmetry hypothesis built in; the explicit case returns $F_{tx} = x$ before and after.

{{< sage exr-gth-F-invariance-sage >}}
:::

The hypothesis of symmetric second derivatives looks technical, but when it fails the field strength acquires a flux concentrated at a point. The third exercise computes that flux for the angle function, the Aharonov-Bohm configuration.

::: {#exr-gth-F-needs-symmetry}
#### A multivalued gauge parameter

In the plane minus the origin let $\theta$ be the polar angle and $\vec A = c\nabla\theta = c(-y, x)/(x^2 + y^2)$. Show
that $\partial_xA_y - \partial_yA_x = 0$ away from the origin, that the circulation $\oint\vec A\cdot d\vec l$ around the
origin is $2\pi c$, and conclude by Stokes' theorem that, as a distribution, $\partial_xA_y - \partial_yA_x = 2\pi
c\,\delta^2(x, y)$: the "pure gauge" $c\nabla\theta$ is a thin flux tube.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_x\bigl(x/(x^2 + y^2)\bigr) + \partial_y\bigl(y/(x^2 + y^2)\bigr) = \bigl((y^2 - x^2) + (x^2 - y^2)\bigr)/(x^2 + y^2)^2
= 0$ for $(x, y) \neq 0$. On the unit circle $\vec A\cdot d\vec l = c\,d\theta$, so the circulation is $2\pi c$ for every
loop around the origin. If the curl were zero as a distribution, Stokes' theorem on a disc would give zero
circulation; so the curl is $2\pi c\,\delta^2$, a flux $2\pi c$ through the origin. The function $\theta$ has
$\partial_x\partial_y\theta \neq \partial_y\partial_x\theta$ there in the sense of distributions, and the proposition does
not apply (@exm-gth-F-lean-reading). A charge $q$ circling the tube acquires the phase $e^{2\pi iqc}$
(@exr-gth-pure-gauge-abelian).
:::

### Yang-Mills theory {#sec-yang-mills}

Replacing the phase rotations of $U(1)$ by a non-abelian group gives gauge fields that carry charge themselves:
their field strength contains a commutator, their equations are nonlinear, and a constant potential can be
curved. Yang-Mills theory is the gauge theory of the Standard Model and the theory that Kaluza-Klein reduction on
a sphere produces in Part IV, and its internal components on a coset space are the Higgs fields of Part V. This
section defines it, with $SU(2)$ as the running example, and computes the field strength and the Bianchi identity
explicitly.

#### Non-abelian gauge fields

For a non-abelian group the gauge parameter is a group-valued function, and the potential takes values in the Lie algebra. The transformation law is fixed by the same requirement as before, that a derivative built from the potential transform like the field; the definition states it, together with its infinitesimal form.

::: {#def-nonabelian-gauge-field}
#### Non-abelian gauge field

For a Lie group $G$ with anti-Hermitian generators $T_a$, $[T_a, T_b] = f_{ab}{}^cT_c$ (@def-structure-constants),
a **non-abelian gauge field** is a Lie-algebra-valued one-form $A_\mu = A^a_\mu T_a$ (@exm-vector-yang-mills) with
the gauge transformation @eq-gauge-transformation, $A_\mu \mapsto g^{-1}A_\mu g + g^{-1}\partial_\mu g$ for $g(x) \in
G$; infinitesimally, $g = e^{\alpha^aT_a}$ gives $\delta A^a_\mu = \partial_\mu\alpha^a + f_{bc}{}^aA^b_\mu\alpha^c$, the
abelian shift plus a rotation in the adjoint representation (@def-adjoint).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The smallest non-abelian group is $SU(2)$, with three generators and the structure constants $\epsilon_{abc}$. The first example counts its gauge fields and identifies them physically.

::: {#exm-nonabelian-su2}
#### $SU(2)$

$A_\mu = A^a_\mu T_a$ with $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ (@eq-su2-brackets): three vector fields, the $W$ bosons of the
weak interaction before symmetry breaking, rotating into each other under the adjoint action of @exm-adjoint-su2.
:::

The strong interaction is the gauge theory of $SU(3)$, and the Standard Model combines three gauge groups. The second example counts their gauge fields.

::: {#exm-nonabelian-su3}
#### $SU(3)$ and the Standard Model

The gluon field $A_\mu = A^A_\mu T_A$ with the eight Gell-Mann generators @eq-gell-mann is the gauge field of the
strong interaction; the Standard Model gauge group $SU(3) \times SU(2) \times U(1)$ has $8 + 3 + 1 = 12$ gauge
fields.
:::

Non-abelian gauge fields also arise from the isometries of an internal space and from higher-dimensional gauge fields. The third example describes both sources, which are the subject of the later parts of the book.

::: {#exm-nonabelian-kk}
#### Kaluza-Klein and coset gauge fields

Reduction on $S^2$ (Part IV) produces an $SO(3)$ gauge field $A^a_\mu$ from the metric components along the three
Killing vectors $K_a$ of @sec-killing, with the structure constants $\epsilon_{abc}$ of @eq-killing-brackets as the
gauge algebra; CSDR (Part V) starts from a Yang-Mills field on $M_4 \times S/R$ in a larger group $G$.
:::

The number of gauge fields is the dimension of the group, which is a quick computation for the classical groups. The first exercise collects the cases that appear in model building.

::: {#exr-gth-gauge-field-count}
#### Counting gauge fields

How many gauge fields do $U(N)$, $SU(N)$ and $SO(N)$ gauge theories have? Evaluate for $SU(5)$ and $SO(10)$, and
check that $SU(3) \times SU(2) \times U(1)$ fits into $SU(5)$ by comparing the numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Lie algebra of $U(N)$ is the space of anti-Hermitian $N \times N$ matrices, of real dimension $N^2$; the
tracelessness condition removes one, so $\dim SU(N) = N^2 - 1$; antisymmetric real matrices give $\dim SO(N) =
N(N - 1)/2$. $SU(5)$ has $24$ gauge fields and $SO(10)$ has $45$. $SU(3) \times SU(2) \times U(1)$ has $12$, and it sits
in $SU(5)$ as the block-diagonal matrices $\operatorname{diag}(U_3, U_2)$ with a compensating phase: the $24 - 12 = 12$
remaining gauge fields are the off-diagonal blocks, $2 \times 3 \times 2$ real components.
:::

The infinitesimal form of the gauge transformation is what one uses in practice, and it follows from the finite one by keeping first-order terms. The second exercise derives it.

::: {#exr-gth-infinitesimal-gauge}
#### The infinitesimal transformation

With $g = 1 + \alpha + O(\alpha^2)$, $\alpha = \alpha^aT_a$, derive $\delta A_\mu = \partial_\mu\alpha + [A_\mu, \alpha]$ from
$A_\mu \mapsto g^{-1}A_\mu g + g^{-1}\partial_\mu g$, and its components $\delta A^a_\mu = \partial_\mu\alpha^a +
f_{bc}{}^aA^b_\mu\alpha^c$. What is it for $U(1)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g^{-1} = 1 - \alpha + O(\alpha^2)$, so $g^{-1}A_\mu g = A_\mu + A_\mu\alpha - \alpha A_\mu + O(\alpha^2)$ and $g^{-1}\partial_\mu g =
\partial_\mu\alpha + O(\alpha^2)$: $\delta A_\mu = \partial_\mu\alpha + [A_\mu, \alpha]$. In components, $[A_\mu, \alpha] =
A^b_\mu\alpha^c[T_b, T_c] = f_{bc}{}^aA^b_\mu\alpha^cT_a$. For $U(1)$ the commutator vanishes and $\delta A = d\alpha$. On a field of
charge $q$ the Lie-algebra-valued potential is $iqA_\mu$ (@def-covariant-derivative-nonabelian), and the rotation
$\phi \mapsto g^{-1}\phi = e^{iq\alpha}\phi$ has the Lie-algebra parameter $-iq\alpha$; so $\delta(iqA_\mu) = -iq\partial_\mu\alpha$,
the shift $A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha$ of @def-gauge-field-u1.
:::

Gauge transformations form a group, and the transformation law must respect the product: transforming twice must equal transforming once by the product. The third exercise checks this with Sage for two non-commuting $SU(2)$ transformations.

::: {#exr-gth-gauge-composition}
#### Gauge transformations compose

Show by hand that $(A^{g_1})^{g_2} = A^{g_1g_2}$, where $A^g = g^{-1}Ag + g^{-1}dg$, and check it with Sage for a general
$SU(2)$ potential in $1 + 1$ dimensions with $g_1 = e^{f(t, x)T_3}$ and $g_2 = e^{h(t, x)T_1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(A^{g_1})^{g_2} = g_2^{-1}(g_1^{-1}Ag_1 + g_1^{-1}dg_1)g_2 + g_2^{-1}dg_2$, and $A^{g_1g_2} = g_2^{-1}g_1^{-1}Ag_1g_2 +
g_2^{-1}g_1^{-1}(dg_1\,g_2 + g_1\,dg_2)$; the two agree term by term. The check uses $e^{\theta T_k} =
\cos\tfrac\theta2 - i\sin\tfrac\theta2\,\sigma_k$.

{{< sage exr-gth-gauge-composition >}}
:::

Matter fields in a representation of the gauge group need a covariant derivative too, and the potential enters through the representation matrices. The definition gives the general form and the adjoint case.

::: {#def-covariant-derivative-nonabelian}
#### Covariant derivative in a representation

A field $\phi$ in a representation $\rho$ of $G$ (@def-representation) transforms as $\phi \mapsto \rho(g)^{-1}\phi$
and its **covariant derivative** is $D_\mu\phi = \partial_\mu\phi + \rho(A_\mu)\phi$, which transforms like $\phi$; for
a field in the adjoint, $D_\mu\Phi = \partial_\mu\Phi + [A_\mu, \Phi]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The doublet of $SU(2)$ is the representation in which the Higgs field of the Standard Model lives. The first example writes its covariant derivative.

::: {#exm-covariant-doublet}
#### The $SU(2)$ doublet

For $\phi \in \mathbb{C}^2$ in the spinor representation, $D_\mu\phi = \partial_\mu\phi + A^a_\mu T_a\phi$ with the
$2 \times 2$ matrices $T_a$: the covariant derivative of the Higgs doublet of @sec-higgs.
:::

Fields in the adjoint representation are matrices, and their covariant derivative involves a commutator. The second example writes it in components and names the adjoint scalars that appear in dimensional reduction.

::: {#exm-covariant-adjoint-scalar}
#### Adjoint scalars

For $\Phi = \Phi^aT_a$, $D_\mu\Phi = \partial_\mu\Phi + [A_\mu, \Phi]$, with components $\partial_\mu\Phi^a +
f_{bc}{}^aA^b_\mu\Phi^c$; the internal components $\phi_a$ of the gauge field in CSDR are adjoint scalars of this kind,
and their potential is built from $[\phi_a, \phi_b]$ (Part V).
:::

As in the abelian case, the commutator of two covariant derivatives contains no derivatives of the field. The third example states the result, which identifies the curvature of the connection.

::: {#exm-covariant-commutator}
#### The commutator of covariant derivatives

$[D_\mu, D_\nu]\phi = \rho(F_{\mu\nu})\phi$ with the field strength of @def-nonabelian-field-strength: the
non-abelian version of @exr-commutator-covariant, and the statement that $F$ is the curvature of the connection
(@def-curvature-connection).
:::

The covariant derivative was defined by its transformation law. The fourth example derives it instead from parallel
transport, the geometric picture behind the name connection, following @nath2017supersymmetry [Sec. 3.1].

::: {#exm-gth-parallel-transport}
#### The covariant derivative from parallel transport

To compare $\phi$ at $x$ and $x + dx$ one first transports $\phi(x)$ to $x + dx$ with the connection, $\tilde\phi(x + dx) = \phi(x) -
\rho(A_\mu)\phi(x)\,dx^\mu$, and then subtracts: both $\phi(x + dx)$ and $\tilde\phi(x + dx)$ transform with $\rho(g(x + dx))^{-1}$, so
their difference does too, and dividing by $dx^\mu$ gives $\partial_\mu\phi + \rho(A_\mu)\phi = D_\mu\phi$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 3.1-3.3,
with Hermitian generators and the coupling $g$ written explicitly]. Transport around a small closed loop then measures
$\rho(F_{\mu\nu})$, as in @exr-gth-int-group-commutator.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

![A non-abelian field strength without derivatives: for the constant $SU(2)$ potential $A_x = c_1T_1$, $A_y =
c_2T_2$ the component $F^3_{xy} = c_1c_2$ over the $(c_1, c_2)$ plane (shading its magnitude, contours its value),
vanishing only on the axes. An abelian constant potential always has $F = 0$. Generated by
`figures/yang_mills_field.sage`.](figures/yang_mills_field.svg){#fig-yang-mills-field width=50%}

For $SU(2)$ the structure constants are those of the vector product, and the adjoint covariant derivative takes a form familiar from mechanics. The first exercise rewrites it in that form.

::: {#exr-gth-adjoint-components}
#### The adjoint of $SU(2)$ in vector notation

For $G = SU(2)$, write $\vec A_\mu = (A^1_\mu, A^2_\mu, A^3_\mu)$ and $\vec\Phi = (\Phi^1, \Phi^2, \Phi^3)$. Show that the
components of $D_\mu\Phi$ are $\partial_\mu\vec\Phi + \vec A_\mu \times \vec\Phi$, and that $D_\mu\Phi = 0$ for $\vec\Phi$
parallel to a constant $\vec A_\mu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[A_\mu, \Phi] = A^b_\mu\Phi^c[T_b, T_c] = \epsilon_{bca}A^b_\mu\Phi^cT_a$, and $\epsilon_{bca}A^b\Phi^c = \epsilon_{abc}A^b\Phi^c =
(\vec A \times \vec\Phi)^a$. If $\vec A_\mu = \vec a_\mu$ is constant and $\vec\Phi = \phi\,\hat n$ with $\hat n$ a constant
unit vector parallel to every $\vec a_\mu$ and $\phi$ constant, both the derivative and the cross product vanish. The
adjoint field rotates under gauge transformations exactly as a vector rotates under $SO(3)$.
:::

The covariance of the doublet covariant derivative under a general $SU(2)$ transformation is the non-abelian analogue of @exr-covariant-derivative-u1. The second exercise checks it with Sage, for a gauge transformation that is a product of two non-commuting factors.

::: {#exr-gth-doublet-covariance}
#### Covariance of the doublet derivative

For a doublet $\phi$ and a general $SU(2)$ potential in $1 + 1$ dimensions, check with Sage that $D'_\mu(g^{-1}\phi) =
g^{-1}D_\mu\phi$ for $g = e^{fT_3}e^{hT_1}$, and show that the ordinary derivative is not covariant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By hand: $\partial(g^{-1}\phi) + (g^{-1}Ag + g^{-1}\partial g)g^{-1}\phi = g^{-1}\partial\phi + (\partial g^{-1})\phi + g^{-1}A\phi +
g^{-1}(\partial g)g^{-1}\phi$, and $\partial g^{-1} = -g^{-1}(\partial g)g^{-1}$ cancels the last term.

{{< sage exr-gth-doublet-covariance >}}
:::

The commutator of covariant derivatives in a representation is the cleanest way to see the commutator term of the field strength. The third exercise derives it for any representation.

::: {#exr-gth-commutator-nonabelian}
#### The non-abelian commutator

Show that $[D_\mu, D_\nu]\phi = \rho(F_{\mu\nu})\phi$ with $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu + [A_\mu,
A_\nu]$, using that $\rho$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_\mu D_\nu\phi = \partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi + \rho(\partial_\mu A_\nu)\phi + \rho(A_\nu)\partial_\mu\phi + \rho(A_\mu)\partial_\nu\phi +
\rho(A_\mu)\rho(A_\nu)\phi$. Antisymmetrising, the second derivatives and the two mixed terms cancel, leaving
$\rho(\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu)\phi + [\rho(A_\mu), \rho(A_\nu)]\phi$, and $[\rho(A_\mu), \rho(A_\nu)] =
\rho([A_\mu, A_\nu])$. For $U(1)$ with $\rho(A) = iqA$ the commutator vanishes and the result is @exr-commutator-covariant.
:::

#### Field strength and action

The commutator found in the last exercise is the new ingredient of the non-abelian field strength. The definition writes it in matrix and component form, and lists its transformation law and its structural identity.

::: {#def-nonabelian-field-strength}
#### Non-abelian field strength

The **field strength** is
$$
F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu + [A_\mu, A_\nu], \qquad
F^a_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A^a_\nu - \partial_\nu A^a_\mu + f_{bc}{}^a A^b_\mu A^c_\nu ,
$$ {#eq-yang-mills-F}
the curvature @eq-curvature-connection of the connection $A$; it transforms covariantly, $F \mapsto g^{-1}Fg$, is
not gauge invariant, and satisfies the **Bianchi identity** $D_{[\rho}F_{\mu\nu]} = 0$ with $D_\rho F_{\mu\nu} =
\partial_\rho F_{\mu\nu} + [A_\rho, F_{\mu\nu}]$. With the coupling made explicit, $A \to gA$, the commutator term
reads $gf_{bc}{}^aA^b_\mu A^c_\nu$ [@alvarezgaume2005, eq. 4.75, Hermitian conventions], the form used in the
proposition below.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The commutator term has a striking consequence: a potential with no derivatives at all can carry a field strength. The first example computes it for two constant $SU(2)$ components.

::: {#exm-su2-constant}
#### An $SU(2)$ field with no derivatives

For $G = SU(2)$, $f_{bc}{}^a = \epsilon_{abc}$. Take the constant configuration $A^1_1 = c_1$, $A^2_2 = c_2$, all
other components zero. The derivative terms vanish and the only non-zero field strength component is the
commutator term, $F^3_{12} = g\,\epsilon_{312}\,c_1c_2 = gc_1c_2$ (and $F^3_{21} = -gc_1c_2$): a constant gauge field can
carry a non-zero field strength (@fig-yang-mills-field, @prp-su2-field-strength, @exr-su2-constant-field), the
first sign that non-abelian gauge fields self-interact. In Part V the internal components of the gauge field on
$S/R$ are constants of exactly this kind, and $F_{ab} = [\phi_a, \phi_b] - f_{ab}{}^c\phi_c$ is the Higgs potential.
:::

Conversely, a potential that is a gauge transform of zero has vanishing field strength, whatever its form. The second example records this, which is the non-abelian version of a pure gauge.

::: {#exm-pure-gauge}
#### Pure gauge fields

$A = g^{-1}dg$ for any $g(x) \in G$ has $F = 0$ by the Maurer-Cartan equation (@exm-mc-equation-curvature,
@exr-yang-mills-equations): it is the gauge transform of $A = 0$, and a flat connection is locally of this form.
:::

The Bianchi identity is the non-abelian form of the homogeneous Maxwell equations. The third example states it in full and names the two facts it rests on.

::: {#exm-bianchi-su2}
#### The Bianchi identity

$D_\rho F_{\mu\nu} + D_\mu F_{\nu\rho} + D_\nu F_{\rho\mu} = 0$ holds for every gauge field, as a consequence of
$d^2 = 0$ and the Jacobi identity of the structure constants (@prp-su2-field-strength, @exr-su2-bianchi): the
non-abelian version of $dF = 0$, which contains the homogeneous Maxwell equations.
:::

For $SU(2)$ the field strength has a vector form in which the commutator becomes a cross product. The first exercise derives it.

::: {#exr-gth-F-components-su2}
#### The $SU(2)$ field strength in vector form

With the notation of @exr-gth-adjoint-components, show that $\vec F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu\vec A_\nu - \partial_\nu\vec A_\mu +
\vec A_\mu \times \vec A_\nu$, and use it to recompute $F^3_{12}$ of @exm-su2-constant with $g = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f_{bc}{}^aA^b_\mu A^c_\nu = \epsilon_{abc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu = (\vec A_\mu \times \vec A_\nu)^a$. For $\vec A_1 = (c_1, 0, 0)$ and
$\vec A_2 = (0, c_2, 0)$ the derivatives vanish and $\vec A_1 \times \vec A_2 = (0, 0, c_1c_2)$, so $F^3_{12} = c_1c_2$ and
the other components of $\vec F_{12}$ vanish.
:::

The covariance of the field strength is what makes the trace of its square a gauge-invariant Lagrangian. The second exercise checks both statements with Sage for a general $SU(2)$ potential in two dimensions.

::: {#exr-gth-F-covariance}
#### Covariance of the field strength

For a general $SU(2)$ potential in $1 + 1$ dimensions and $g = e^{fT_3}e^{hT_1}$, check with Sage that $F'_{tx} =
g^{-1}F_{tx}g$, that $F_{tx}$ itself changes, and that $\operatorname{Tr}(F_{tx}F_{tx})$ does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The commutator term $[A'_t, A'_x]$ produces the terms that cancel the inhomogeneous pieces $g^{-1}\partial g$ of the
derivative terms, leaving $g^{-1}Fg$; the trace is invariant by its cyclicity.

{{< sage exr-gth-F-covariance >}}
:::

Since $F$ is not gauge invariant, one might hope to remove the field strength of a constant potential by a clever gauge transformation. The third exercise shows that gauge invariants forbid it.

::: {#exr-gth-F-not-invariant}
#### A field strength that cannot be gauged away

Show that $\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma})$ is gauge invariant for all index values. Deduce that the constant
potential of @exm-su2-constant is not gauge equivalent to $A = 0$ when $c_1c_2 \neq 0$, and that it is not gauge
equivalent to an abelian potential $A_\mu = a_\mu T_3$ with constant $a_\mu$ either.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{Tr}(g^{-1}F_{\mu\nu}g\,g^{-1}F_{\rho\sigma}g) = \operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma})$ by cyclicity. For the
constant potential $\operatorname{Tr}(F_{12}F_{12}) = g^2c_1^2c_2^2\operatorname{Tr}(T_3T_3) = -\tfrac12g^2c_1^2c_2^2 \neq 0$,
while $A = 0$ and every constant abelian potential have $F = 0$ and hence a vanishing invariant. Gauge
transformations cannot change the value of an invariant, so no gauge transformation relates them: the field
strength of a constant non-abelian potential is physical.
:::

The kinetic term of the gauge field is the gauge-invariant square of its field strength. The definition fixes the normalisation and the sign appropriate to anti-Hermitian generators and the signature $(+, -, -, -)$.

::: {#def-yang-mills-action}
#### Yang-Mills action

The **Yang-Mills action** is
$$
S = \frac{1}{2g^2}\int d^4x\,\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) = -\frac{1}{4g^2}\int d^4x\,F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu}
$$ {#eq-yang-mills-action}
with $\operatorname{Tr}(T_aT_b) = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$ (@prp-su2-structure), gauge invariant because the trace is
invariant under conjugation; it is the normalisation of @alvarezgaume2005 [eq. 4.79] once $gA \to A$, with the
**gauge coupling** $g$ multiplying the cubic and quartic self-interactions. Its Euler-Lagrange equations are the
**Yang-Mills equations** $D_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = 0$, nonlinear, and the same expressions hold in any dimension, which is how
they appear on $M_4 \times S/R$ in Part V.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The field equations of the action are the non-abelian Maxwell equations, with the gauge field acting as its own source. The first example writes them in components.

::: {#exm-ym-equations}
#### The Yang-Mills equations

$\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu\,a} + f_{bc}{}^aA^b_\mu F^{\mu\nu\,c} = 0$: the gauge field is a source for itself, since it
transforms in the adjoint representation; the constant potential of @exm-su2-constant does not solve them
(@exr-yang-mills-equations), while every pure gauge does.
:::

When the group is abelian every commutator vanishes, and the construction must reduce to electromagnetism. The second example confirms that it does.

::: {#exm-ym-abelian-limit}
#### The abelian limit

For $G = U(1)$ the structure constants vanish, @eq-yang-mills-F is $dA$, the action is Maxwell's
@eq-maxwell-action and the equations are linear: Yang-Mills theory contains electromagnetism as its abelian
special case.
:::

The same action makes sense in any dimension, and on a product space it splits according to the directions of the indices. The third example describes the splitting, the origin of a Higgs sector in dimensional reduction.

::: {#exm-ym-reduction}
#### The action on a product space

On $M_4 \times S/R$ with coordinates $(x^\mu, y^a)$ the components of $F$ split into $F_{\mu\nu}$, $F_{\mu a}$ and
$F_{ab}$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(F^2)$ into a four-dimensional Yang-Mills term, kinetic terms for the internal
components and a potential $\operatorname{Tr}(F_{ab}F^{ab})$: the Higgs sector of CSDR, derived from this action in
Part V.
:::

The sign of the action is fixed by requiring positive energy, and with anti-Hermitian generators the trace is negative, which is why the action has a plus sign in front of the trace. The first exercise checks the signs.

::: {#exr-gth-ym-energy-sign}
#### The sign of the Yang-Mills action

Define $E^{a\,i} = F^{a\,i0}$ and $B^{a\,i} = -\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F^a_{jk}$. Show that $-\tfrac14F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu} =
\tfrac12\sum_a(\vec E^a\cdot\vec E^a - \vec B^a\cdot\vec B^a)$ in $(+, -, -, -)$ and that
$\tfrac{1}{2g^2}\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$ equals $-\tfrac{1}{4g^2}F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu}$. What would go wrong
with $-\tfrac{1}{2g^2}\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For each $a$ the computation is that of @exr-gth-maxwell-from-fields: $F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu} = -2\vec E^a\cdot\vec E^a +
2\vec B^a\cdot\vec B^a$. With $\operatorname{Tr}(T_aT_b) = -\tfrac12\delta_{ab}$, $\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) =
-\tfrac12F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu}$, so $\tfrac{1}{2g^2}\operatorname{Tr}(FF) = -\tfrac{1}{4g^2}F^aF^a = \tfrac{1}{2g^2}\sum_a(\vec E^a
\cdot \vec E^a - \vec B^a\cdot\vec B^a)$. The opposite sign would give the electric fields a negative kinetic energy: the
Hamiltonian would be unbounded below and the theory would have ghosts.
:::

The Yang-Mills equations are nonlinear, and a quick way to see it is to test them on the simplest non-abelian configurations. The second exercise does this with Sage.

::: {#exr-yang-mills-equations}
#### Pure gauge and the Yang-Mills equations

With Sage, check that $A = g^{-1}dg$ has vanishing field strength for $g = e^{f(t, x)T_3}$, and evaluate the
Yang-Mills equations on the constant potential of @exm-su2-constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-yang-mills-equations >}}
:::

Expanding the action in powers of the potential shows the self-interactions explicitly: a cubic term with one derivative and a quartic term without derivatives. The third exercise identifies the quartic term with Sage.

::: {#exr-gth-ym-cubic-quartic}
#### The quartic self-interaction

With the coupling explicit, $F^a_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A^a_\nu - \partial_\nu A^a_\mu + g\epsilon_{abc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu$ for
$SU(2)$. Show that $-\tfrac14F^aF^a$ is a sum of a quadratic term (Maxwell's, for each $a$), a cubic term proportional
to $g$ and a quartic term proportional to $g^2$, and check with Sage that for constant fields
$$
-\tfrac14F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu} = -\tfrac{g^2}{4}\left[(\vec A_\mu\cdot\vec A^\mu)^2 - (\vec A_\mu\cdot\vec A_\nu)(\vec A^\mu\cdot\vec A^\nu)\right].
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Writing $F = F_{\rm lin} + gF_{\rm quad}$, $-\tfrac14F^2 = -\tfrac14F_{\rm lin}^2 - \tfrac g2F_{\rm lin}\cdot F_{\rm quad} -
\tfrac{g^2}{4}F_{\rm quad}^2$: the cubic term has one derivative and three potentials, the quartic none and four. For
constant fields only $F_{\rm quad} = \vec A_\mu\times\vec A_\nu$ survives, and the Lagrange identity $(\vec a\times\vec
b)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d) = (\vec a\cdot\vec c)(\vec b\cdot\vec d) - (\vec a\cdot\vec d)(\vec b\cdot\vec c)$ gives the formula.
The quartic potential is non-negative for purely spatial constant fields, and it vanishes exactly when all the
$\vec A_i$ are parallel, the abelian configurations.

{{< sage exr-gth-ym-cubic-quartic >}}
:::

The Yang-Mills Lagrangian determines an energy density, and in the temporal gauge it takes the familiar form of the
energy of electric and magnetic fields. The fourth exercise derives it from the Lagrangian, as @nath2017supersymmetry
[Problem 3.6] does for the coupled Yang-Mills-Dirac system.

::: {#exr-gth-ym-energy}
#### The Yang-Mills energy density

Define $E^a_i = F^a_{0i}$ and $B^a_i = -\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F^a_{jk}$. Show that $-\tfrac14F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(\vec E^a\cdot\vec E^a -
\vec B^a\cdot\vec B^a)$, and that in the temporal gauge $A^a_0 = 0$ the canonical energy density is $\tfrac12(\vec E^a\cdot\vec E^a + \vec B^a\cdot\vec B^a)
\geq 0$, where $\vec B^a$ now contains the term quadratic in the potential.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the signature $(+, -, -, -)$, $F^{a\,0i} = -F^a_{0i}$ and $F^{a\,ij} = F^a_{ij}$, so $F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu} = -2\sum_iF^a_{0i}F^a_{0i} +
\sum_{i,j}F^a_{ij}F^a_{ij} = -2\vec E^a\cdot\vec E^a + 2\vec B^a\cdot\vec B^a$, using $\sum_{i,j}F_{ij}F_{ij} = 2\vec B\cdot\vec B$ for an antisymmetric
$F_{ij} = -\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. In the temporal gauge $F^a_{0i} = \partial_0A^a_i$, so the momentum conjugate to $A^a_i$ is
$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial(\partial_0A^a_i) = E^a_i$ and the energy density $E^a_i\partial_0A^a_i - \mathcal{L}$ is $\vec E^a\cdot\vec E^a - \tfrac12(\vec E^a\cdot\vec E^a - \vec B^a\cdot\vec B^a) = \tfrac12(\vec E^a\cdot\vec E^a + \vec B^a\cdot\vec B^a)$.
The magnetic field $B^a_i = -\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F^a_{jk}$ is the curl of $\vec A^a$ plus
$-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}f_{bc}{}^aA^b_jA^c_k$, so even a constant potential carries energy, as in @exm-su2-constant [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 3.155].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In Euclidean signature the action is a sum of squares, and completing the square bounds it from below by a term that
depends only on the topology of the field. The fifth exercise derives the bound and its equality case, the self-dual
fields [@nath2017supersymmetry, Problem 3.2].

::: {#exr-gth-self-dual-bound}
#### The self-duality bound

In four Euclidean dimensions let $\tilde F^a_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^a_{\rho\sigma}$. Show that $\tilde{\tilde F} = F$ and
$F^a_{\mu\nu}F^a_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(F^a \mp \tilde F^a)_{\mu\nu}(F^a \mp \tilde F^a)_{\mu\nu} \pm F^a_{\mu\nu}\tilde F^a_{\mu\nu}$, and deduce that the
Euclidean action $\tfrac{1}{4g^2}\int F^a_{\mu\nu}F^a_{\mu\nu}$ is at least $\tfrac{1}{4g^2}|\int F^a_{\mu\nu}\tilde F^a_{\mu\nu}|$, with equality exactly
for self-dual or anti-self-dual fields.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tilde{\tilde F}_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac14\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\epsilon_{\rho\sigma\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\beta} = \tfrac14 \cdot 2(\delta_{\mu\alpha}\delta_{\nu\beta} -
\delta_{\mu\beta}\delta_{\nu\alpha})F_{\alpha\beta} = F_{\mu\nu}$, and the same contraction gives $\tilde F_{\mu\nu}\tilde F_{\mu\nu} = F_{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$.
Expanding, $\tfrac12(F \mp \tilde F)^2 = \tfrac12(F^2 + \tilde F^2) \mp F\tilde F = F^2 \mp F\tilde F$, which is the identity. The square is
non-negative, so $\int F^2 \geq \pm\int F\tilde F$ for both signs, that is $\int F^2 \geq |\int F\tilde F|$, with equality when $F = \pm\tilde F$
pointwise [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 3.150]. By the next exercise $\int F\tilde F$ is the integral of a total divergence and
depends only on the behaviour at infinity: self-dual fields, the instantons, minimise the action in each topological
class.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The density $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma})$ can be added to the Lagrangian with a coefficient $\theta$ without
changing the field equations, because it is a total divergence. The sixth exercise identifies the divergence, the
Chern-Simons current, and checks the identity by machine [@nath2017supersymmetry, Problem 3.3 and eq. 6.119].

::: {#exr-gth-theta-total-derivative}
#### The $\theta$ term is a total divergence

For $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu + [A_\mu, A_\nu]$, show that $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\operatorname{Tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}) =
\partial_\mu K^\mu$ with $K^\mu = 4\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\operatorname{Tr}(A_\nu\partial_\rho A_\sigma + \tfrac23A_\nu A_\rho A_\sigma)$, and check it with Sage for an
$SU(2)$ potential whose components are random quadratic polynomials.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding $F$, the term with four potentials vanishes, $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\operatorname{Tr}(A_\mu A_\nu A_\rho A_\sigma) = 0$, because cycling the
trace moves the first factor to the end, an odd permutation of the four indices. The rest is $4\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}(\partial_\mu A_\nu
\partial_\rho A_\sigma) + 4\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}(\partial_\mu A_\nu A_\rho A_\sigma)$. On the other side, $\partial_\mu(\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}A_\nu\partial_\rho A_\sigma) =
\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}\partial_\mu A_\nu\partial_\rho A_\sigma$ (the second derivatives cancel by antisymmetry), and $\partial_\mu(\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}A_\nu A_\rho
A_\sigma) = 3\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}(\partial_\mu A_\nu A_\rho A_\sigma)$ by cyclicity, so the factor $\tfrac23 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 8$ must match $2 \cdot 4$
from $\epsilon\operatorname{Tr}(\partial A\,[A, A])$: the coefficient $\tfrac23$ is forced. In forms this is $\operatorname{Tr}F^2 = d\operatorname{Tr}(A\,dA +
\tfrac23A^3)$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 6.119]. The machine confirms it, and that the identity fails without the cubic
term:

{{< sage exr-gth-theta-total-derivative >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The field strength of the constant configuration and the Bianchi identity for every configuration are the two results of this section checked as exact identities. The proposition states them for $SU(2)$ with the coupling made explicit, as polynomial identities in the potential and its first and second derivatives.

::: {#prp-su2-field-strength}
#### Field strength and Bianchi identity of $SU(2)$

On the constant configuration of @exm-su2-constant, $F^3_{12} = gc_1c_2$, $F^3_{21} = -gc_1c_2$ and $F^1_{12} = F^2_{12}
= F^3_{03} = 0$. For every $SU(2)$ gauge field and coupling, $D_\rho F^a_{\mu\nu} + D_\mu F^a_{\nu\rho} + D_\nu
F^a_{\rho\mu} = 0$, as a polynomial identity in the jets $A$, $\partial A$, $\partial\partial A$ (symmetric second
derivatives), by the Jacobi identity of $\epsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Polynomial identities in the jet variables.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.FieldTheory.su2_field_strength >}}

**Sage.** Pending.

The listed vanishing components each have a simple reason, and checking them by hand is a good test of the index conventions. The first example goes through them.

::: {#exm-gth-su2-prp-components}
#### Why the other components vanish

In the constant configuration only $A^1_1$ and $A^2_2$ are non-zero. $F^a_{\mu\nu}$ is antisymmetric in $\mu\nu$, so
$F^3_{21} = -F^3_{12}$. $F^1_{12} = g\epsilon_{1bc}A^b_1A^c_2$ needs $b, c \in \{2, 3\}$, but $A^2_1 = A^3_1 = 0$; similarly
$F^2_{12}$ needs $A^1_2$ or $A^3_2$, both zero. $F^3_{03}$ involves $A_0$ and $A_3$, which vanish. Only the pair $(b, c) =
(1, 2)$ with $\mu = 1$, $\nu = 2$ contributes, giving $F^3_{12} = gc_1c_2$.
:::

The proposition uses the Hermitian convention with an explicit coupling, while the definitions use anti-Hermitian generators; the two must be translated consistently. The second example spells out the dictionary.

::: {#exm-gth-su2-prp-conventions}
#### The two conventions

With Hermitian generators $t_a = \tfrac12\sigma_a$, $[t_a, t_b] = i\epsilon_{abc}t_c$, and the potential $\mathcal{A}_\mu =
\mathcal{A}^a_\mu t_a$ enters as $D_\mu = \partial_\mu - ig\mathcal{A}_\mu$. Since $T_a = -it_a$, $-ig\mathcal{A}^at_a =
g\mathcal{A}^aT_a$, so the anti-Hermitian potential of @def-nonabelian-gauge-field is $A^a_\mu = g\mathcal{A}^a_\mu$, and
$F^a = g(\partial_\mu\mathcal{A}^a_\nu - \partial_\nu\mathcal{A}^a_\mu + g\epsilon_{abc}\mathcal{A}^b_\mu\mathcal{A}^c_\nu)$.
The bracket in parentheses is the Hermitian field strength, which is the form of the proposition.
:::

In the abelian limit the Bianchi identity must reduce to the homogeneous Maxwell equations. The third example writes them out in terms of $\vec E$ and $\vec B$.

::: {#exm-gth-bianchi-abelian}
#### The homogeneous Maxwell equations

For $U(1)$, $D_\rho = \partial_\rho$ on $F$ and the identity is $\partial_\rho F_{\mu\nu} + \partial_\mu F_{\nu\rho} +
\partial_\nu F_{\rho\mu} = 0$. With $(\rho, \mu, \nu) = (1, 2, 3)$ it is $-\nabla\cdot\vec B = 0$, using $F_{12} = -B^3$
and its cyclic partners (@exr-gth-maxwell-from-fields); with one time index, $(0, i, j)$, it is Faraday's law
$\partial_t\vec B + \nabla\times\vec E = 0$. These are the two Maxwell equations that do not involve the sources.
:::

The constant configuration is the first concrete computation of a non-abelian field strength. The first exercise computes all its components, by hand and with Sage.

::: {#exr-su2-constant-field}
#### A constant non-abelian field

Compute all components of $F^a_{\mu\nu}$ for $A^1_1 = c_1$, $A^2_2 = c_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only $F^3_{12} = g\epsilon_{312}A^1_1A^2_2 + g\epsilon_{321}A^2_1A^1_2 = gc_1c_2$ survives, with $F^3_{21} = -F^3_{12}$.
In Sage:

{{< sage exr-su2-constant-field >}}

:::

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.FieldTheory.su2_field_strength >}}

The Bianchi identity holds for every field, and it is instructive to see it hold for a field with derivatives in all directions. The second exercise checks all components for an explicit potential.

::: {#exr-su2-bianchi}
#### The Bianchi identity on an explicit field

For $A^1_1 = xy$, $A^2_2 = t\sin z$, $A^3_3 = e^x$, compute $F$ and check $D_{[\rho}F_{\mu\nu]} = 0$ for all index
values.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The field strength has derivative terms ($F^1_{01} = -\partial_1 A^1_0 + \dots$) and the commutator term
$F^3_{12} = g\,xy\,t\sin z$; the Bianchi identity holds component by component, as it must for any field. In
Sage (all 192 components):

{{< sage exr-su2-bianchi >}}
:::

The algebraic reason behind the Bianchi identity is the Jacobi identity, and isolating its role is the content of the third exercise. It sorts the terms of the cyclic sum by the number of potentials they contain.

::: {#exr-gth-bianchi-jacobi}
#### The Bianchi identity from the Jacobi identity

Expand $\sum_{\rm cyc}D_\rho F_{\mu\nu} = \sum_{\rm cyc}(\partial_\rho F_{\mu\nu} + [A_\rho, F_{\mu\nu}])$ for $F = dA + [A, A]$
and show that the terms with no potential undifferentiated cancel by symmetry of second derivatives, the terms with
one differentiated and one undifferentiated potential cancel in pairs, and the terms with three potentials cancel by
the Jacobi identity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Terms in $\partial\partial A$: $\sum_{\rm cyc}\partial_\rho(\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu) = 0$ since each $\partial_\rho\partial_\mu A_\nu$
appears once with each sign. Terms in $A\,\partial A$: from $\partial_\rho[A_\mu, A_\nu]$ come $[\partial_\rho A_\mu, A_\nu] +
[A_\mu, \partial_\rho A_\nu]$, and from $[A_\rho, \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu]$ come $[A_\rho, \partial_\mu A_\nu] - [A_\rho,
\partial_\nu A_\mu]$; under the cyclic sum, $[A_\mu, \partial_\rho A_\nu]$ from the first cancels $-[A_\mu, \partial_\rho A_\nu]$
coming from the second with $(\rho, \mu, \nu) \to (\mu, \nu, \rho)$, and similarly for the other pairs. Terms in $AAA$:
$\sum_{\rm cyc}[A_\rho, [A_\mu, A_\nu]] = 0$, the Jacobi identity. For $SU(2)$ the last statement is $\epsilon_{abe}\epsilon_{ecd} +
\epsilon_{bce}\epsilon_{ead} + \epsilon_{cae}\epsilon_{ebd} = 0$, which is the content of @prp-su2-field-strength.
:::

#### Anomaly coefficients

A gauge theory with chiral fermions, left- and right-handed Weyl spinors in different representations, is
consistent as a quantum theory only if a cubic invariant of its fermion representations vanishes. The quantum origin
of the condition, the anomaly, was outlined in quantum field theory (@def-chiral-anomaly); the invariant itself is pure group theory,
and this subsection defines it and computes it for the groups used so far [@nath2017supersymmetry, Secs. 6.1 and
6.9].

::: {#def-gth-anomaly-coefficient}
#### Anomaly coefficient

Let left-handed Weyl fermions (@def-dq-weyl-equation) transform in a representation $\rho$ of a compact gauge group $G$
(@def-representation), and let $t_a = i\rho(T_a)$ be the Hermitian generators. The **anomaly coefficient** of $\rho$ is the totally
symmetric tensor
$$
d_{abc}(\rho) = \operatorname{Tr}\bigl(t_a\{t_b, t_c\}\bigr) ;
$$ {#eq-gth-anomaly-coefficient}
for $G = U(1)$ and charges $q_k$ it is $2\sum_kq_k^3$. A right-handed fermion in $\rho$ counts as a left-handed fermion in the
**conjugate representation** $\bar\rho(g) = \rho(g)^*$, whose Hermitian generators are $-t_a^T$. A gauge theory is free of gauge
anomalies only if the sum of $d_{abc}$ over all its left-handed fermions vanishes (@def-anomaly).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The abelian case shows the content of the condition most simply. The first example compares a single charged Weyl
fermion with the Dirac fermion of quantum electrodynamics.

::: {#exm-gth-anomaly-u1}
#### Charged Weyl fermions
